title: Taking amrit
hookLine: the initiation, given by five Sikhs, is a serious personal step, never pressed on anyone

lines: A QUIET ROOM, A STEEL BOWL.
cards: A quiet room. Five people standing. A steel bowl of water, and a double-edged sword moving through it slowly.

For the person who has come to take amrit, this is a promise thought about for weeks, sometimes years, then said aloud in front of people who matter. Nobody can sign you up for it. Nobody is supposed to push you into it.

teach.b: Amrit means the nectar of immortality. Sanchar means bringing it into being, passing it on. Together, amrit sanchar is the Sikh initiation, also called khande di pahul, the initiation of the double-edged sword.

It goes back to Vaisakhi, 1699, at Anandpur. Guru Gobind Singh stirred water in an iron bowl with a khanda, a double-edged sword. Tradition says Mata Sahib Kaur added sugar puffs, so the steel would carry sweetness too.
He gave it to the first five, the panj pyare, the five beloved ones. Then, in the tradition's telling, came the surprise. He asked the five to give it to him.
The Guru, with folded hands, received it from the people he had just initiated. Today's ceremony keeps that shape.

teach.h: THE GURU ASKS THE FIVE TO INITIATE HIM.
teach.b: Five initiated Sikhs, standing in for the panj pyare, prepare the amrit while reciting five prayers from the Sikh daily prayers, including Guru Nanak's Japji.

The person taking it drinks from cupped hands, and it's sprinkled on the eyes and the hair. They greet each other: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. The Khalsa belongs to God, and so does the victory.
They're taught the code: the five Ks, the daily prayers, and yesterday's four things avoided. It's a real commitment, and Sikhs treat it that way.
People take amrit at different ages: some as teenagers, some in their forties, some never.

teach.h: A STEP TAKEN WHEN YOU'RE READY.
teach.b: The Sikh code of conduct says anyone of any background who is ready to live by the vows may take it. The word that matters is ready. Amrit isn't handed out to fill a room.
It's a step a person chooses when the promise is theirs.

how: Amrit sanchar is held in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib, usually in a gurdwara, where five initiated Sikhs prepare amrit in an iron bowl while reciting five banis; those who take it commit to the five Ks, daily prayer and the Rehat.

s: every Sikh takes amrit as a baby
people take it when they're ready: as teenagers, as adults, or not at all.
the ceremony is given by five initiated Sikhs
they stand in for the panj pyare, the first five of 1699.
the Guru gave amrit but never received it
tradition says he asked the first five to initiate him in turn.

games.q: Anandpur, 1699. you're the Guru. you've just initiated the first five. what next?
o: stand above them as their commander.
ask the five to give amrit to you.
send them home and close the ceremony.
games.why: tradition says Guru Gobind Singh asked the five to initiate him. the teacher took the step his students took.

practice: Think of one commitment in your life, one you made or one you're still weighing, and ask it three honest questions: is this mine, or am I doing it because someone expects it; what would it ask of me on an ordinary Tuesday; and what would keeping it give back.
You don't have to decide anything now; just let the questions sit, the way the five let the water be stirred slowly.

wordCard.voice: Amrit sanchar. The Sikh initiation, given by five initiated Sikhs, with water stirred by a double-edged sword. A serious step, chosen, never pressed.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: amrit, the nectar of immortality; sanchar, bringing it into being and passing it on.

carryVoice: Your line: a step, not a pressure. A yes means most when there was room to say not yet. That's day two hundred seventy-one.
